extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating diagnostic-method claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for purposive construction of diagnostic-method claims: how to identify the problem solved, determine the inventor's solution (essential elements), and use that construction to assess statutory subject‑matter, novelty and obviousness. Intended to be applied by examiners (and relied upon by applicants/practitioners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The identification of the problem and the solution provided by the invention informs the purposive construction of the claims. An identification of the problem is guided by the description and the examiner's understanding of the common general knowledge in the relevant art. Examiners should bear in mind that an application may describe more than one problem to be solved. For diagnostic methods, it may be appropriate to consider that an inventor is generally looking to solve a data acquisition problem and/or a data analysis problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the specification and the common general knowledge (CGK) of the person of ordinary skill (POSITA) to identify the problem. Recognize multiple problems may be present; for diagnostics, explicitly consider whether the problem is a data acquisition problem (practical means to obtain data about an analyte) and/or a data analysis problem (intellectual correlation/interpretation of data). Use the description's emphasis and CGK to guide which problem(s) are at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors indicating a data acquisition problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a data acquisition problem exists, the description will typically describe technical matter that goes beyond the common general knowledge (CGK) of the skilled person in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors in the description that may indicate the existence of a data acquisition problem include disclosure of: a novel or non‑CGK analyte; a novel or non‑CGK combination of biomarkers; a novel or non‑CGK means to identify or quantify an analyte (regardless of whether the analyte itself was known or CGK); applying a CGK means to a sample or subject population that is not standard to that means; performing a CGK means within specific non‑standard constraints (e.g., timing); explicit statements that a specific problem or solution relates to how to identify or quantify an analyte; a significant level of detail on technical aspects of how data about the analyte is acquired; and/or emphasis on challenges or deficiencies of prior means to identify or quantify the analyte.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors suggesting a data analysis problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors in the description that may suggest that a data analysis problem exists include: explicit statements suggesting the problem to be solved is a data analysis problem; placing an emphasis on discovery of an allegedly new correlation between a condition and an analyte with relative absence of technical details about how to acquire the data; indicators that, to acquire data about the analyte, it is CGK to apply the means contemplated by the application; and/or absence of any explicit indication that practical problems were overcome relating to how to acquire data about an analyte that is CGK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification emphasizes correlations/interpretation rather than technical acquisition, treat the invention as solving a data analysis problem. The relative lack of acquisition detail and the existence of CGK acquisition methods point toward data‑analysis being the core problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the solution to the identified problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution is the element or set of elements that is essential to the successful resolution of the problem. If a claim includes solutions to more than one problem, examination should focus on one solution to a problem in performing the purposive construction. The initial choice of solution should be guided by the description, selecting the solution given the greatest emphasis by the inventors. If it becomes necessary to consider a different solution, the analysis should be undertaken anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which claim elements provide the solution to the selected problem (the 'essential elements'). Where multiple problems/solutions appear, pick the one receiving greatest emphasis in the disclosure and analyse that; if later another solution must be considered, restart the purposive construction for that solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative examples of data acquisition elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a data acquisition problem has been identified, the solution is provided by those elements that provide a means to acquire data about an analyte. The means by which the data is acquired may be represented by either a single step or by multiple steps within the diagnostic claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative claim steps that indicate data acquisition elements include: detecting protein X in a subject sample; measuring the concentration of substrate X; determining expression levels of genes A, B and C; contacting a urine sample with antibody A and determining optical density at 450 nm; incubating a sample with a nucleic acid probe (e.g., SEQ ID NO:1) and detecting hybridization to target sequence Z. These steps typically supply tangible, physical steps that supply statutory subject‑matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative examples of data analysis elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a data analysis problem has been identified, the solution is provided by those elements that relate to the analysis of acquired data for the purpose of providing diagnostic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative claim steps that indicate data analysis elements include: relating presence of protein X from a test sample to a diagnosis; comparing expression levels of genes to a control standard (e.g., decrease indicates disease Y); conditional thresholds (e.g., if sample value >0.24 then disease Y suspected); interpreting hybridization as indicative of presence of disease Y. Such elements may be mental, conceptual, or interpretive in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposive construction (interpretation and essentiality determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Having identified the problem and solution, a purposive construction of the claims involves: interpreting the meaning of the various terms used therein; and determining whether elements in the claims are essential (provide the solution to the identified problem) or non‑essential (do not provide the solution to the identified problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform claim term interpretation in light of the specification and CGK, then mark which elements are essential because they provide the solution. Use this construction to determine the inventive concept and to assess statutory subject‑matter, novelty and obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between data acquisition and data analysis elements (aggregation vs combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizing that how data is analyzed or interpreted in a diagnostic method generally has no material effect on how the data needs to be physically acquired (and vice versa), the data acquisition elements and data analysis elements in the diagnostic method claim likely have a relationship reflecting an aggregation rather than a combination. Thus, the solution to a problem will be provided by either data acquisition elements or data analysis elements, but not both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat acquisition and analysis steps as aggregated (co‑present) rather than synergistically combined for the purpose of determining which elements provide the inventive concept. Typically only one class (acquisition or analysis) will constitute the essential solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining whether a claim defines statutory subject‑matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A diagnostic claim construed as being limited to essential elements that are disembodied (e.g., mental process, lacking physicality, no practical application, etc.) will be identified as defective for not complying with section 2 of the Patent Act because the subject‑matter does not fall within a category of invention as defined in section 2. By contrast, data acquisition elements likely define statutory subject‑matter since they usually relate to tangible (non‑disembodied) practical steps which fall within a category of invention as defined in section 2. Thus, where such a data acquisition element is identified as an essential element of the construed claim, the claimed subject‑matter will likely be statutory unless the claim includes excluded subject‑matter, such as a method of medical treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the essential elements are purely disembodied analysis/mental steps, conclude the claim may not be statutory under s.2. If essential elements are concrete acquisition steps, the claim will likely be statutory, but still check for other exclusions (e.g., medical treatment). Use the purposive construction to identify which side applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the essential elements to define the inventive concept for novelty and obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Once essential elements (the solution) are identified, the inventive concept of the claim includes those essential elements. Novelty and obviousness analyses should be performed with respect to that inventive concept: whether a single prior art disclosure discloses and enables the essential elements (anticipation), and whether the inventive concept would have been obvious to the POSITA in light of the prior art and CGK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the inventive concept (essential elements) to prior art documents. A prior art disclosure that discloses and enables the essential elements anticipates the claim. For obviousness, determine whether the POSITA, in light of CGK and prior art, would have arrived at the inventive concept without invention. Where data acquisition is the inventive concept, prior art that teaches the same means to acquire the specific data will defeat novelty/obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: POSITA and Common General Knowledge (CGK) identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The POSITA is defined relative to the field and may be a team (examples include combinations of clinicians, geneticists, molecular biologists, medical technologists, toxicologists, endocrinologists, microbiologists, etc.). The CGK consists of knowledge in the relevant field at the claim date (e.g., known genes, public sequence databases, known assay techniques, commercial microarrays, epidemiological links).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly define the POSITA team and the CGK for each case (use the specification and prior art to support this). Use CGK to determine whether elements (analytes, methods, correlations) were known or routine, which affects whether the identified problem is acquisition or analysis and how inventive the solution is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when claims implicate both acquisition and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claims include both data acquisition and data analysis elements related to medical diagnoses, the purposive construction analysis should identify which elements provide the solution to the identified problem; elements providing the solution are essential, others may be non‑essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If acquisition elements provide the solution, treat those as essential and evaluate statutory subject‑matter and patentability accordingly. If analysis elements provide the solution, be alert to statutory subject‑matter concerns (disembodied mental steps). Example guidance: in mixed claims, acquisition steps may be essential while the interpretive use of the acquired data might be non‑essential to the inventive concept.
